name: Parrot OS
summary: A security-oriented GNU/Linux distribution based on Debian, engineered for penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, digital forensics, software development, and privacy protection.
license: GPL-3.0-or-later and upstream open-source tool licenses

content.introduction: Parrot OS is an open-source Linux distribution engineered for cybersecurity professionals, penetration testers, forensic analysts, reverse engineers, and privacy advocates. Founded in 2013 by Lorenzo Faletra and developed under the Frozenbox project (subsequently structured as the Parrot Security team), Parrot OS combines a hardened operating system environment with a curated collection of security evaluation tools. Built on the Debian GNU/Linux package ecosystem, Parrot OS provides a turnkey testing and development platform delivered across multiple desktop editions, virtual appliances, container images, and cloud deployments.
content.what_is_it: Technically, Parrot OS is a Debian-derived distribution tracking Debian Stable (Debian 12 Bookworm in the 6.x release cycle) coupled with custom security software repositories, patched Linux kernels, and native configuration suites. Unlike general-purpose distributions, Parrot OS optimizes its system configuration for audit workflows, low-resource hardware efficiency, and traffic anonymization. Key distinguishing subsystems include AnonSurf (an operating-system-level Tor routing orchestrator), custom AppArmor profiles, modular metapackages, integrated container virtualization via Docker and Podman, and the PipeWire multimedia architecture.
content.origin_and_history: The Parrot OS project originated in Italy in 2013, created by Lorenzo Faletra alongside an international community of open-source contributors and security practitioners. Initially conceived as a lightweight penetration testing system based on Debian, early versions utilized custom scripts and light desktop components. Over successive release milestones (Parrot 3.x, 4.x, and 5.x), the distribution refined its core repository infrastructure, replaced legacy audio subsystems with PipeWire, integrated the Calamares graphical installer, and standardized on Debian Stable as its base to minimize dependency conflicts. The Parrot 6.x series (code-named 'Lory'), introduced in 2024 and maintained through subsequent point updates such as 6.4 in 2025 and 2026, upgraded the core base to Debian 12 Bookworm, introduced experimental containerization for security utilities, and phased out legacy 32-bit x86 ISO builds in favor of x86_64 and ARM64 architectures.
content.governance_and_community: Parrot OS is organized and maintained by the Parrot Security team, a distributed collective of core developers, package maintainers, and security researchers led by founder Lorenzo Faletra. Infrastructure, build servers, repository mirrors, and documentation platforms are financed through community donations, hardware sponsorships, and commercial support partnerships. Development activities, issue tracking, and packaging recipes are conducted openly on the project's GitLab organization under `gitlab.com/parrotsec`. The project coordinates software updates and packaging decisions through public discussions, maintaining transparency regarding code modifications, package signing keys, and repository governance.
content.debian_stable_base_and_rolling_updates: Parrot OS implements a hybrid release model combining the foundational stability of Debian Stable with rolling updates for security utilities and kernels. The core operating system files, system libraries, and desktop environment packages derive directly from Debian Stable repositories, ensuring system predictability and preventing packaging breakage. In parallel, the Parrot Security team maintains dedicated upstream mirrors and backports repositories that continuously update security assessment utilities (such as Metasploit, Nmap, Wireshark, and Burp Suite) and hardware kernel drivers independently of Debian's point-release calendar.
content.editions_and_deployment_profiles:
Parrot OS is officially distributed in several purpose-built editions:

- Parrot Security Edition: The flagship penetration testing environment, pre-installed with over 600 specialized tools for web application auditing, network reconnaissance, cryptography analysis, exploitation, and digital forensics.
- Parrot Home Edition: A streamlined, lightweight daily operating system intended for standard desktop usage, privacy-focused web browsing, secure communication, and software development, excluding the heavy security auditing suites by default.
- Parrot Hack The Box (HTB) Edition: A tailored environment developed in partnership with the Hack The Box cybersecurity training platform, pre-configured with VPN access profiles and targeted practice tooling.
- Parrot Cloud and Architect Editions: Minimal, headless root filesystem images designed for cloud VPS hosting, container runtimes, embedded platforms, and custom minimal desktop assembly.
content.desktop_environments_and_interface: The default desktop interface for Parrot OS Security and Home editions is the MATE desktop environment, complemented by an officially supported KDE Plasma edition. The MATE edition is customized with a dark theme, custom icon sets, hierarchical application menus categorized by cybersecurity workflow phases (Information Gathering, Vulnerability Analysis, Web Applications, Exploitation Tools, Post Exploitation, Password Attacks, Wireless Attacks, Reverse Engineering, and Forensics), and system status applets. KDE Plasma editions provide modern graphical effects and Wayland compositor compatibility for users requiring advanced desktop scaling and visual customizability.
content.anonsurf_and_privacy_routing: A central architectural component of Parrot OS is AnonSurf, a system-wide privacy utility developed natively in C and shell scripts by the Parrot Security team. AnonSurf redirects all outbound operating system network traffic through the Tor onion routing network using local `iptables` and `nftables` firewall rules. When activated, AnonSurf tunnels TCP connections, intercepts and routes DNS queries through DNSCrypt or Tor resolve listeners, and blocks non-Tor UDP packets to prevent accidental IP address leakage. AnonSurf also includes an integrated emergency killswitch and IP status monitor accessible via terminal commands (`anonsurf start`, `anonsurf stop`, `anonsurf status`) or graphical desktop applets.
content.kernel_architecture_and_wireless_drivers: Parrot OS ships with a custom-built Linux kernel (tracking upstream kernel branches including Linux 6.5 and 6.12 LTS) compiled with specific security enhancements, AppArmor mandatory access control enforcement, and out-of-tree hardware patches. The kernel package incorporates driver patches enabling promiscuous packet capture (monitor mode) and raw 802.11 wireless frame injection across numerous Wi-Fi network interface cards (NICs), supporting wireless security assessments and protocol audits without manual kernel recompilation.
content.tool_ecosystem_and_containerization: The Parrot Security Edition aggregates more than 600 security assessment utilities. To resolve dependency friction between legacy Python 2 libraries, competing Ruby environments, and modern toolchains, the Parrot 6.x release cycle introduced containerized tool execution. Complex or rarely used testing frameworks can be executed inside isolated Docker or Podman containers managed via helper scripts, preventing system library pollution and keeping the underlying base operating system lean. Package management is handled natively through Debian's APT framework and dpkg, supplemented by Flatpak support for sandboxed desktop software.
content.live_boot_and_calamares_installer: Parrot OS ISO images operate as hybrid bootable live media supporting both BIOS and UEFI systems (including UEFI Secure Boot compatibility via Debian-signed shim loaders). The live environment allows direct execution in system RAM without writing to host storage. For permanent installation on physical drives, solid-state media, or external drives, Parrot OS employs the Calamares graphical system installer. Calamares supports manual partition layouts, automated storage partitioning, and integrated full-disk encryption backed by LUKS2 (Linux Unified Key Setup) and dm-crypt.
content.arm64_and_wsl_support: In addition to standard 64-bit x86_64 desktop and server architectures, Parrot OS provides official images for ARM64 single-board computers (such as the Raspberry Pi 4 and 5) and virtualized environments. Parrot OS is also packaged for the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), allowing security analysts and developers on Windows workstations to execute Parrot CLI tools and launch graphical sessions via X11 or Wayland display servers without dual-booting.
content.threat_model_and_operational_limits:
Parrot OS provides an integrated platform for security audits and privacy defense, but its technical documentation clarifies the boundaries of its threat model:

- Monolithic Kernel Architecture: Parrot OS is a monolithic Linux distribution; a vulnerability or kernel exploit executed by a compromised application grants system-level access, contrasting with hypervisor-isolated environments like Qubes OS.
- AnonSurf Operational Limits: While AnonSurf redirects network traffic through Tor, it does not rewrite application-level metadata or eliminate browser fingerprinting characteristics unless paired with dedicated privacy browsers like Tor Browser.
- Authorized Use: Penetration testing tools included in Parrot OS can cause system instability or legal liabilities if executed without explicit written authorization against target networks and systems.
- Persistent Footprint: Unlike amnesic systems like Tails, standard installed instances of Parrot OS retain logs, history, and configuration files unless explicitly run in ephemeral live mode with RAM wiping.
content.privacy_and_telemetry: Parrot OS enforces a strict non-commercial, zero-telemetry policy. The operating system contains no centralized user tracking, advertising identifiers, or background telemetry services sending operational data to remote servers. All software package updates, repository index downloads, and mirror synchronizations occur via standard HTTP/HTTPS channels over APT without hardware identifiers or license validation tokens. Users may configure APT to fetch package updates exclusively over Tor onion mirrors for enhanced repository anonymity.
advantages: Stable foundation based on Debian Stable, preventing system breakage while delivering updated security tools
Native integration of AnonSurf for system-wide Tor traffic redirection and DNS leak prevention
Comprehensive software inventory featuring over 600 pre-installed tools for penetration testing and digital forensics
Multiple official editions (Security, Home, HTB, Architect) tailored to distinct use cases from desktop computing to servers
Calamares graphical installer supporting full-disk encryption with LUKS2 out of the box
Official support across x86_64, ARM64 (Raspberry Pi), and Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)
Lightweight resource footprint with customized MATE and KDE desktop interfaces
disadvantages: Monolithic Linux architecture lacking the hardware-enforced hypervisor isolation of Qubes OS
Installed system is not inherently amnesic like Tails; logs and bash histories persist on disk unless running in Live RAM mode
Large download footprint for the full Security Edition ISO (exceeding 5 GB of storage space)
AnonSurf tunnels general TCP/UDP traffic but does not automatically strip application-layer telemetry or browser fingerprints
Steep learning curve for inexperienced users unfamiliar with Linux terminal operations and security tooling
who_is_it_for: Penetration testers, ethical hackers, and red teamers conducting authorized vulnerability assessments and network audits
Digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) specialists requiring data acquisition and carving utilities
Cybersecurity students, CTF participants, and Hack The Box practitioners practicing in simulated lab environments
Software developers, reverse engineers, and system administrators seeking a stable Debian-based workstation with security tool access
who_is_it_not_for: Users seeking an amnesic, zero-footprint live system by default for sensitive whistleblower communication (better suited to Tails)
Users requiring compartmentalized virtual domains to execute untrusted malware samples (better suited to Qubes OS)
General non-technical computer users seeking a simple plug-and-play desktop operating system
Legacy 32-bit computer hardware (support deprecated in the Parrot 6.x series)

components.name: AnonSurf Module
components.note: Native iptables and nftables orchestrator routing operating-system traffic and DNS through the Tor network.

components.name: Hardened Linux Kernel
components.note: Custom-compiled kernel with AppArmor support and wireless 802.11 monitor mode and frame injection drivers.

components.name: Calamares Installer
components.note: Modular graphical installation framework supporting automated LUKS2 disk encryption configuration.

components.name: MATE Desktop Environment
components.note: Lightweight, customizable graphical user interface featuring categorized penetration testing tool menus.

components.name: Parrot Metapackage Architecture
components.note: Structured package collections (parrot-tools-full, parrot-interface, parrot-crypto) managing security toolsets.

components.name: PipeWire Audio Infrastructure
components.note: Modern low-latency multimedia routing framework replacing legacy PulseAudio and ALSA daemons.

relations.name: Debian
relations.note: Upstream operating system foundation; Parrot OS utilizes Debian Stable repositories for core packages.
